name: THE WHAT IF PEAPOD WAS ONE OF US BURGER

recipe.history:
The garden pea — Pisum sativum — is a plant with one of the most storied scientific histories of any food crop on earth. Cultivated since Neolithic times in the Near East and the Fertile Crescent, it traveled westward with the expansion of agriculture and was among the first vegetables grown in medieval European monastery gardens, where it fed monks through long winters as a dried legume. But the pea's most consequential role in history may be scientific rather than culinary: Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar working in Brno in the 1860s, used garden peas to articulate the foundational laws of genetics, tracking the inheritance of traits like seed color and wrinkled versus smooth coats across generations of plants in his monastery garden. Fresh pea purée — the specific preparation at the heart of this burger — is a French technique from the classical brigade tradition, where petits pois à la française were puréed with butter and seasoned with mint and salt to produce a vivid green sauce of extraordinary sweetness and color, used as a base for fish and lamb in haute cuisine.

Pea purée arrived in the American burger world through the British pub burger tradition, where mushy peas — a rougher, more rustic cousin of the French purée — had long accompanied fish and chips and eventually migrated to the burger as a topping that no American would have predicted but many fell immediately in love with. The sweetness of the peas, their bright vegetal flavor, and the way a well-made purée holds its green color under the slight warmth of a beef patty made them a natural partner for beef, especially when enriched with butter and mint. As American gastropubs began importing British pub food aesthetics in the 2010s, the pea purée burger acquired a legitimate American following, and chefs began playing with it — adding lemon zest, crème fraîche, wasabi — refining a preparation that had started as something almost accidental into something deliberately composed.

The first time I made pea purée at home, I was following a recipe that told me to add only a small amount of butter. I followed the instruction and produced something that tasted like baby food. On my second attempt I added three times as much butter as the recipe called for, borrowed a trick from the French tradition of mounting a sauce at the last moment with cold cubed butter, whisking it in over low heat until the purée became glossy and velvety and impossibly rich. The color brightened as if someone had turned a dial. I ate most of it standing at the stove with a spoon, and I felt the specific satisfaction of having fixed a mistake by committing harder to the principle that was causing the mistake in the first place. More fat. More patience. More respect for the ingredient.

A medium rare burger — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is the correct temperature for a pea purée burger for a reason that is almost too obvious to state but too important to omit: the purée is cold or at most room temperature when it hits the patty, and the warmth of the meat is what brings it to life. At 54–57°C, the beef still carries residual heat enough to take the slight chill off the purée and soften the butter within it without cooking the delicate pea flavor away. A well-done patty would be too dry and its heat too residual to do anything useful; an under-cooked patty would be too cool to warm the purée at all. Medium rare is the temperature at which these two things find each other and become one dish.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
2 tbsp fresh mint leaves, finely chopped
Salt and white pepper to taste
Salt and white pepper to taste
900g freshly ground beef (80% chuck, 20% brisket blend)
6 slices young Pecorino or mild Manchego cheese
1 small head butter lettuce, leaves separated
instructions: 1. Make the pea purée: Bring a medium saucepan of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Add peas and blanch for 90 seconds until bright green and just tender. Drain immediately and transfer to a bowl of ice water for 1 minute to stop the cooking and preserve the color. Drain and transfer to a blender. Add smashed garlic and 60ml cold water. Blend on high until very smooth. While the blender is running on low, add cold cubed butter piece by piece, allowing each cube to incorporate before adding the next, to mount the purée into a glossy, velvety sauce. Add fresh mint, lemon zest, and lemon juice. Season generously with salt and white pepper. Pass through a fine-mesh sieve for an ultra-smooth texture if desired. Keep warm in a small saucepan on the lowest heat, stirring occasionally.
2. Make the lemon crème fraîche: Stir together crème fraîche, lemon zest, lemon juice, and honey until combined. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.
3. Cook the crispy pancetta: Lay pancetta slices in a cold non-stick skillet and heat to medium. Cook, turning once, for 3–4 minutes per side until crisp and golden. Drain on paper towels.

4. Make the brioche buns: Combine bread flour, instant yeast, salt, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl with a dough hook. Add 2 eggs and warm milk, mix on low for 2 minutes, then knead on medium for 5 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time. Knead on medium-high for 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.

5. Place dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 6 portions of about 100g, shape into tight balls, place on parchment-lined baking sheets, and proof covered for 45 minutes.
6. Preheat oven to 190°C (375°F). Brush buns with egg wash (remaining egg plus 1 tablespoon water) and bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

7. Form the beef patties: Divide ground beef into 6 equal portions of 150g. Handle minimally. Form each into a 10cm-wide, 2cm-thick patty with a thumb indent in the center. Season both sides with salt and cracked black pepper immediately before cooking.

8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties dry and undisturbed for 3 minutes. Flip once. Place a slice of Pecorino or Manchego on each patty immediately. Cook for 2–2.5 more minutes. Confirm internal temperature of 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes.
9. Slice brioche buns and toast cut-side down in a buttered skillet over medium heat for 60–90 seconds.

10. Assemble each burger: Spread lemon crème fraîche on both cut faces of the bun. Place a butter lettuce leaf and two tomato slices on the bottom bun. Set the rested cheese-topped patty on top. Spoon a generous mound of warm pea purée directly over the patty. Top with 1–2 slices of crispy pancetta and a scattering of blanched whole peas. Finish with flaky sea salt and the top bun. Serve immediately.
